utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. We are back again to continue our case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The case is IT-95-14/1-T, Tribunal versus Zlatko Aleksovski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Will the Prosecution make their appearances.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, my name is Niemann, and I appear with my colleague, Mr. Meddegoda, for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Niemann. And for the defence, Mr. Mikulicic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I am Goran Mikulicic and I appear with my colleague Mr. Joka for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good morning to the interpreters and our sound engineers, Mr. Mikulicic, you have called another witness for today, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. The Defence will invite witness Mr. Darko Kristo, who is sitting here now, and we will start with questioning of witnesses for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kristo. Will you please stand up? You will now read the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: You may be seated, and you will now answer the questions which Mr. Mikulicic will ask you. Mr. Mikulicic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Mikulicic

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kristo, my name is Mikulicic, and I represent the accused Zlatko Aleksovski. On behalf of the Defence, I will pose you the questions and I appeal for you to answer them to the best of your memory. I also kindly ask you to speak slowly so that we can allow the interpreters to translate what you will be saying. Mr. Kristo, tell us when and where were you born?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: On the 3rd of August, 1965, in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you go to school?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: In Zenica, at the elementary school in Busovaca and secondary school in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kristo, what kind of secondary school did you attend in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: A school for catering personnel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember, when did you complete schooling?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes. In 1983.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, after completing secondary school, find a job, or did you continue your schooling? What did you do after graduation?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: I immediately found a job.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember where was that?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: In a company called Tisa Tourist, a catering company in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you found a job in the catering industry?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kristo, in what capacity did you work there?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: As a waiter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Until when did you work as a waiter in Tisa Tourist?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Until 1991, the end of 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you stop working? You stopped working then?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us why.

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Because I volunteered for the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was in 1991, the end of that year, when a war broke out in Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you volunteered for the HVO; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Kristo, when you joined HVO, did you take part in some armed actions or did you work somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: I worked as a cook.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you work as a cook in 1991?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: At the Tisa Hotel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But as a military personnel?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember, Mr. Kristo, in which military unit you then served as a cook?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: It was the Nikola Srbinski (phoen) unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And until when did you serve as a cook at the Tisa Hotel?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: It was just for a short period after which we left for the Draga barracks and then to the Kaonik barracks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you arrive in Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: In 1992, in October 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kristo, you told us that you grew up and went to school in Busovaca, so I suppose then that you know the area around Busovaca; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what was the purpose of the Kaonik facility before the war broke out in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: A military police unit was deployed there, and I personally know, as a cook, that we were deployed there because of military police to put the kitchen into operation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You did not understand me, Mr. Kristo, so I will have to repeat the question. Before the war broke out in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1990 and in 1980, what was the purpose of the Kaonik barracks? Who was there?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: The Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it then correct that Kaonik was a barracks of the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you at that time, when the Yugoslav People's Army was at Kaonik, did you have a chance to visit that facility?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you came there for the first time only after you had joined the HVO and served there as a cook; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that was in October 1992?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Kristo, when you arrived in the Kaonik area, where was the kitchen situated?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: At the very entrance to the barracks. The first building some 10 metres away from the gate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember who was there in that building?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes. Military police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the kitchen was situated or located in the first building near the gate where military police were also deployed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that correct, that it was your duty to prepare food for military police?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Kristo, when or whether, within the Kaonik facility, a district military tribunal was formed; do you know that?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: It was set up but only after the new year or around the new year. I can't remember exactly the date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that in the building in which you were located as a cook or where the military police was located or in another building?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: In another building up there in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When this district military prison was set up at the end of 1992 and 1993, did you prepare food for the prisoners as well?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Kristo, where did you get the raw materials for cooking?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: From Draga.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what Draga is?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: It is the barracks where the commanders were located, the regiment commanders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From the barracks, the raw materials were brought to you and you prepared food and meals from those raw materials; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember approximately what kind of food was that?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Well, just like for any other kitchen. In the beginning, there was everything that we needed until regular supplies were possible, potato, macaroni, meat, lentils, peas, and things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe, Mr. Kristo, what kind of a kitchen was that, what kind of equipment was there in the kitchen?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Well, it was not a proper kitchen as far as I know what kitchens should be like, but from the Tisa Hotel, we took some of the inventory and then we made a kitchen there for military police in order to prepare food, like stoves, utensils, and similar things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, Mr. Kristo, when you arrived there in the building where the military police were also located, there was not a kitchen before in that building, but you had set it up; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you had to take care to bring the necessary equipment for the kitchen in order to prepare food?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you had a stove on which you cooked food. What kind of a stove was that?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Electricity stove.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many plates were there; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Four.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you prepared food on those four plates?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that sufficient capacity-wise to prepare food for military police, I mean the period before armed conflicts broke out in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes, as far as military police is concerned, yes, it was sufficient.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many meals a day did you prepare?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember now. It was a long time ago. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you because we want to hear whether you prepared just lunch or breakfast and lunch and maybe dinner. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: We prepared breakfast, lunch, and dinner, and sometimes we served canned food for breakfast, like pate, like fish, or ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that true that you had prepared three meals out of which sometimes not all of them were cooked meals and breakfast was canned food?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kristo, do you remember when armed conflicts broke out in the Busovaca territory area between Muslims and Croats?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: I think it was in January. I can't remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in that period, you were working in the kitchen; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, while working in the kitchen, feel that there was an increased need for food or the quantity of food that you had to prepare? Did you, after armed conflicts broke out in Busovaca, did you have to prepare more food than before?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us why?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Because the district prison was set up there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So simply there were more people for whom you had to prepare food?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Kristo, that at the end of January 1993 in the Kaonik facility that a group of civilians was brought from Busovaca and they were temporarily accommodated there; do you know that?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you prepare food for those people as well?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have, Mr. Kristo, because of an increased number of people, did you have to bring some more kitchen equipment, or was the equipment there sufficient for that purpose?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: No, it was not sufficient, especially as far as utensils were concerned, so we asked the regiment to bring us a kitchen in which we could prepare food outside. We used an open heat stove outside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did they bring you this equipment?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: To the best of their potential, the basic equipment that we asked for was there, the trailer was brought, which we used as a kitchen, but other equipment was not sufficient.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you speak about the inventory and utensils, what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Well, I mean like plates and forks and things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The small inventory, as you call it, or as far as I remember, you said that you brought it from the Tisa Hotel?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kristo, you said that a trailer was brought. Can you tell us what kind of a trailer was that? Was that sort of a kitchen mess?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it was a kitchen mess with three big cauldrons inside, I don't know how many auxiliary pieces were there, and we used timber and wood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it is an auxiliary kitchen which the army usually uses when they are in the field; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was brought near to where you had been accommodated. Where was it exactly?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Behind our building, behind our kitchen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kristo, did somebody help you in the preparation of the food or did you do it alone?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: I was a cook together with another one, and when the number of people increased, when the Muslim civilians arrived, then we sought help from Zlatko as far as the prisoners up there were concerned, and these were the people from the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if I understood you correctly, when the number of people was increased for which you had to prepare food, then you asked help or you asked to be given more people in order to prepare more food?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the people that were given to you as help, they were Croatian soldiers who were disciplined at the district military prison; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Kristo, now we are speaking about the period when the Muslim civilians were brought to Kaonik and when you had to prepare food for them as well, so we are referring to this period. Mr. Kristo, did you, under those conditions, prepare three meals a day or not?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So three meals a day?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Until regular supplies were possible, three meals a day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, was it sufficient?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: What can I tell you? When supplies were regular, we had enough food for all of us because it was not only the civilians, Muslims, but the army as well, and ourselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you prepared food which was also served to the prisoners in the district prison and the Muslims which were brought, the civilians which were brought, and who else?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Military police and the guards, of course, and we also prepared food for outside the barracks, for the frontline, and for some other outlets in the city, in the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it then correct, Mr. Kristo, that at the place where you prepared food, from there it was distributed to the prison, to the fighters who were on the defence lines, and to some facilities in the town, and that it was the same food?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that correct then, that the guards and prisoners had the same food?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: The same. Everybody ate the same food because there was no possibility to prepare different types of food and kinds of food because there were too many people for the capacity of our kitchen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. So the food was the same, and the meals, quantity-wise, were the same, or did you have different quantities of food or meals for guards and for prisoners or ...

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: It was the same for all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Kristo, in the situation where supplies were more or less regular, did the prisoners have the possibility to ask for more helpings if it was possible?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes, yes, in all circumstances, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kristo, do you remember that, in the kitchen or as a consequence of the intake of food that you had prepared, that some people would have some stomach problems, that people would feel sick because of that?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Nothing like that had happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kristo, in which way was the food from the kitchen where it was prepared taken to the prison where the prisoners were located?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: The Muslims, accompanied by guards, would come to the kitchen and then take up the food to the prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any opportunity to go to that prison or did you stay in the lower building all the time?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Because of my job, I had to remain down there all the time, and I just -- I think I might have gone there, up once or twice, but under extraordinary circumstances.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was under extraordinary circumstances. It was not a regular occurrence?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kristo, you also said that the prisoners or the Muslim civilians who were brought to Kaonik, that they would come to take the food. Then you would have had the opportunity to see them?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did they look to you? Were they underfed, were they in a terrible state as far as hygiene was concerned?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: To me, normally. I didn't see anything unusual.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kristo, I'm aware of the fact that you stayed in the lower building and that you were preoccupied with your job, but let me ask you, nevertheless, the following: Do you know perhaps when the Muslim civilians from the Busovaca area were brought to Kaonik? Do you remember, when was that?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Well, it might have been in January. I can't remember the exact date. At the end of January.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Maybe the beginning of February.

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, it has been six years since then and it's only normal. Do you remember then, Mr. Kristo, how long they stayed in Kaonik? How long did you have to prepare more food? Do you remember how long was that?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly the date, it was such a long time ago. Well, perhaps until Easter time when the exchange took place. I can't remember on which date the Easter holidays were at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kristo, you said that you belonged to the regiment so you were not a member of the military police in whose building you actually stayed.

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But do you know what unit did the guards at the district prison belong to? Did they belong to your regiment or were they members of the military police; do you know that?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Military police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you meet Mr. Zlatko Aleksovski at that time when you were at Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you meet him once or several times?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Several times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you recognise him if you saw him today?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I see him over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Please, may I state for the record that the witness is pointing at the accused, Zlatko Aleksovski.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kristo, do you remember when it was the first time you saw Mr. Zlatko Aleksovski, under what circumstances? I'm not asking you about the date?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Well, it could have been towards the end of January, perhaps in the beginning of February.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember perhaps what Mr. Zlatko Aleksovski wore at the time? How was he dressed? Military or civilian?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Well, anyhow, I mean, sometimes he wore civilian clothes, sometimes a uniform, sometimes it was a combination of civilian trousers and an army upper part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kristo, how were you dressed? Were you in civilian clothes or were you in a uniform? I understand, of course, that when you cooked, you wouldn't be wearing it, but will you tell me?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: I wore jeans, and, of course, I had a white coat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The cook's --

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the guards in Kaonik, were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: They wore uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they have any insignia? Did they have patches? Did they have MP indicated on their sleeves or something, the guards?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You do not remember or what?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kristo, do you remember Mr. Zlatko Aleksovski having any insignia on those occasions when he had a uniform on?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: No, no, none.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He did not have any insignia. And rank, what about rank indication?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kristo, do you remember perhaps if you provided adequate quantities of tea for people accommodated in the prison for their daily consumption? Did you issue some excessive quantities of tea or normal?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: No, just normal with breakfast, one usually got either tea or coffee with milk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. And tea and coffee brought along with other food from the Draga barracks or did you have another source of supply?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: From the Draga barracks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A little while ago, you mentioned that at a certain point in time, it was very difficult to get supplies. What does that mean? What does it mean? Why were the supplies any more difficult?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Well, probably because we were surrounded and there was not enough food.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I guess the lines of communication were cut off?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did you manage then?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Well, I think for a certain period of time, I think for about a month, we kept it to two meals a day, that is, because there was a shortage of food, so we simply eliminated one meal a day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did it apply to all or only to some?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: To all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did you get meat or was there some livestock around, were there some cattle around or what?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes, if there was no meat at the regiment -- I mean, if there was not fresh meat, if there was not fresh meat, there was some tinned meal and the like, some goulash tins and things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did it ever happened that the local population brought their live stock to be slaughtered for the needs of the canteen?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: I did not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember seeing that the soldiers brought their livestock from their own farms to provide meat for the kitchen; did these things happen?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kristo, you repeatedly mentioned -- repeated that food was brought over from the Draga barracks. Does it mean that their driver brought it?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes. The driver from Draga brought the food and he also distributed that food that we cooked there, that we prepared, took it to the frontline and to the outposts in the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know perhaps which were those outposts in the town?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: The post office, the medical centre, and a couple of policemen at some checkpoints, and I guess there was some other places but I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Kristo, if the prisoners could prepare the tea for themselves in the -- on the premises of the prison or perhaps in the canteen?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: I do not know because I was in a different part of the building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kristo, will you please try to jog your memory and remember under what circumstances did you have contact with Mr. Aleksovski, what were these contacts about?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Well, man to man. There was no business talks because there was no need to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if I understood you properly, those were the common kind of contacts, not any kind of military contacts or official contacts?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: No, they were not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware that Mr. Aleksovski -- if Mr. Aleksovski was a member of the military police in that building in which you were?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how Mr. Aleksovski treated the prisoners or those interned Muslim civilians who were accommodated there; do you know that?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: I never went upstairs, and I think that Zlatko always treated everyone correctly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you have no personal knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kristo, you mentioned that you were surrounded and that the lines of communication were cut off and that supplies were rendered very difficult; is that true?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So at that time what was the security situation at Kaonik itself? Did it ever happen that Kaonik would be fired at?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember any of such incidents when Kaonik was exposed to fire? Do you remember something happening?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: I remember Ivica Bazaric (phoen), a Domobran who was wounded there. I don't remember the date, because I was the one who gave the first aid, who bandaged him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned Ivica Bazaric, a Domobran. What was he doing in Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: I think he was there at the entrance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a visitor or a guard?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Guard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did I understand you properly? He was a guard at the entrance door?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes, of the prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that door is right next to the door to the canteen; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Well, about 10 metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Bazaric was wounded at that place as a guard?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what he was -- how was he wounded, a shell or a bullet or what?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: A shell hit the place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what were his injuries?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't know. Doctors would know it. But I know where the wound was and I had to bandage it and that was over the kidneys, somewhere in the kidney area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you extended first aid to him?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember if somebody else was wounded during such incidents?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: With him, there was another one, he was Saro (phoen), I can't remember his first name, but he was wounded too. He was also a guard, another Domobran, and he was with Ivica Bazaric at the gate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recall if any of the prisoners were wounded; did that happen?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I assume, but please correct me if I am wrong, Mr. Kristo, that in those days, the defence lines were very near the Kaonik facility since the shells were falling around it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you know how close the defence line was to the frontline, to Kaonik, I mean?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: You mean the distance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but perhaps a kilometre or two, I wouldn't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kristo, where do you work now?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Privately, Busovaca, in a private restaurant, Europa.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you are not with HVO anymore?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you leave HVO?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The Defence has no further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mikulicic. Mr. Niemann or Mr. Meddegoda, do you have any questions for this witness? Cross-examined by Mr. Meddegoda

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Just a few questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kristo, you said that there were civilians who were brought to the kitchen, escorted by the guards to take the food?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you know any of those Muslim civilians who came to the kitchen to take the food?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Of course, I did, because they were friends of long standing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they were from Busovaca, as far as you remember?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they were all law-abiding, good citizens of the community, as yourself?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Well, how law been abiding they were, I wouldn't know, but before the war, yes, we led the same life.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But as far as you know, they were good citizens of the community, as far as you are aware?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know why they were being detained at the Kaonik barracks, at the Kaonik prison?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also said that there were times when the equipment you had was not sufficient to cope with the cooking -- with the cooking demand, for the cooking needs?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: I didn't understand you, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was a time when you sought help from the -- from Mr. Aleksovski with regard to obtaining more cooking facilities?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: From Mr. Aleksovski? No, I asked for men, I asked for some assistance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who did you ask for assistance?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Well, those prisoners, those who were there because of some disciplinary transgressions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I know. They were the prisoners. Whom did you ask for that assistance, from whom did you obtain permission to get that assistance?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: You mean down there, from the personnel?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Well, I said, yes, from Zlatko or the shift leader if Zlatko was not there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who the shift leader was? Do you recall who the shift leader was? Do you recall the names of the shift leaders?

utterances.speaker: DARKO KRISTO
utterances.text: I don't. It was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, have you any more questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, we have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Kristo, you have just finished giving your testimony here. We have no further questions for you, and therefore thank you for coming and we wish you a nice return home. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Defence would like to call its next witness, Mr. Janko Batinic. (The witness entered)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. It is me who is talking to you. Can you hear me? You will now read the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Are you all right? Are you comfortable?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: You will now answer the questions which Mr. Mikulicic will pose to you. Examined by Mr. Mikulicic

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Batinic. I am Goran Mikulicic, and here I am representing the interests of Mr. Aleksovski, my client. I have some questions relating to the indictment, and I should like you to answer them to the best of your recollection. Mr. Batinic, will you tell us where and when were you born?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: I was born in the municipality of Busovaca in the village of Carica, on the 29th of June, 1944.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Batinic, have you always lived in the area or not?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this is the area of the municipality of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your ethnic origin?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: I am a Croat by origin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your religion?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: A Catholic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where and when did you attend school, Mr. Batinic?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: In 1963, I graduated from the teachers' school in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And elementary school?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: In Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you get a job after completing the teachers' school?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember your first job?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes. My first job was in a village in the territory of Busovaca which was 100 per cent Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what kind of a job did you have there?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: I was headmaster.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after that ...

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: I then moved into the municipal government.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Until when were you a teacher, a headmaster?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Until 1965.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that after 1965, you moved and you went to work for the municipal authorities. Could you please describe it?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: I became the head of the Territorial Defence command at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that it was back in 1965; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Batinic, do you remember that it was during the former Yugoslavia. So, Mr. Batinic, do you remember what was the task of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: The task of the Territorial Defence was the reserve formation which would perhaps take part in case of a war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Batinic, did you serve the army?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I served the JNA in the reserve officers school at Bilica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember when that was?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you reach a rank?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes, a Major, I became a Major, but that was later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Batinic, do you recall the beginning of armed conflicts in the territory of the Municipality of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Of course I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us what it is that you remember about that? When did it happen?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Well, it was in '92, the second conflict.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were you doing? Where were you at that time?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: I was an officer in the Croatian Defence Council, in the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But were you still an active officer or were you retired at that time?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: I was retired.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Batinic, were you a retired military person or were you a civilian pensioner?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: I was pensioned off as a civil servant, as a municipal civil servant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In other words, as a civil servant; is that so?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, despite the fact that in 1993, you were retired, that you were a civilian at that time, you nevertheless volunteered for the Croatian Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were you deployed? Where were you posted?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: The defence line facing Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Batinic, were you throughout the first semester of 1993 on the same positions, or were you moved somewhere?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: I was there until the end of February '93 and then I was sent elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that other post, where was that that you went at the end of February '93?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: I became the commander of the company, of the company which was formed in the area and which was autonomous in the territory of Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I think there was a slight error in translation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you tell us what you were?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: I was deputy commander of the company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you said that this company was a Domobran company?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For clarification sake, will you please tell us what kind of an army unit is it and who was it made of?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: The basic purpose of this Domobran company was because we felt that Busovaca would be blocked off shortly because there were no young men there as they were all on the defence line and we decided that we had to do something to help defend Busovaca, and so we agreed to form that company. Its principal task was to secure all facilities in the territory of Busovaca which were of any relevance to the defence of Busovaca, such as bridges, then other important objects, such as the medical centre, the post office, the security of the hospital, the health centre, night patrols, because there were not enough military police around the town, so we organised night patrols around the town to prevent plunder and subversive activities, and we also secured some plots of land where we sowed potatoes and wheat so as to feed the population during the blockade, because we knew that famine could easily set in, that our children might starve, and so we tried to secure these things so as to survive through the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Batinic, what was the composition of this Domobran company?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: This Domobran company was made of young men who could carry arms under law and all those people of elderly age who could go to the defence line, so we even had those who were 75 years old included in our company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any uniforms or ...

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: No. They mostly wore civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any weapons?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did, but those were ordinary hunting rifles, shotguns and such, a few pistols, and perhaps some old automatics, Russian ones.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In other words, if I have understood you properly, Mr. Batinic, the principal task of this new military unit was security?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes, but we also secured the prison, that is, the entrance to the prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What prison do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: The district prison, Kaonik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so, Mr. Batinic, at that time, those young men, able-bodied men, were on the defence lines; is that so?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And other young men who could not do the army duty became members of the Domobran company; is that true?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes, but not all of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How strong was that company; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. It had some 80 to 100 men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many objects did that company, that is its men, secure?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: About 20 objects.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do? Did you take shifts or what?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: In shifts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long was one shift and how many men?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Every shift was two men strong, and they were four-hour shifts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does that mean? Four hours on guard and then a rest?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes, then the second shift would come, but that was only at night-time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Batinic, apart from those elderly persons and those young men who were not deemed as capable of carrying weapons and who yet made up this Domobran company, were there some other people in the territory of Busovaca who did not join the company and yet were not on the defence lines? Were there any such men?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Batinic, do you know what those people did during the armed conflicts? What was their duty? I mean, those who were neither involved with the HVO nor with the HVO company.

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Well, at times they helped those who were at the defence line, that is, took food to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there also some instances where those people were under labour obligations?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were those labour obligations?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Digging out trenches.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were those people who were thus obligated from the territory of the Municipality of Busovaca? Were they the citizens of the Croat ethnic origin, of Serb ethnic origin, or Muslim, or all of them?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: All of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Batinic, how were they called up for this labour obligation? How did they go there?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: They were called up by the defence office, and that was their labour obligation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Batinic, you mentioned that the company that you were the deputy commander of also secured -- guarded the prison at Kaonik; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many sentries, how many guards were there on a shift at Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: There were eight guards at the entrance, at the gate, to the object, to that facility where the prison was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember perhaps when it was that your company began to secure that facility where Kaonik was? When was it?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: As far as I can -- as far as I remember, it was sometime from February onward.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What year are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You personally, were you also at Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In what capacity?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Deputy commander of the company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do there? Also for security reasons or something else?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: I was the deputy commander, so it was my duty to do rounds of my men by day and by night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Batinic, does that mean that you visited Kaonik relatively frequently?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us if the members of the Domobran company guarded only the entrance to Kaonik or did they also guard objects within Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: For a while, they also guarded the prison within the facility, but only in the surroundings, not inside, and subsequently they withdrew to the entrance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not sure I really understood you. Did they guard the facility, outside the facility, or were they outside?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: They were on the outside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your rounds in Kaonik, have you had the opportunity of meeting Mr. Aleksovski?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you meet him once or several times?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Several times. We cooperated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you recognise Mr. Aleksovski if you saw him today?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Of course, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: For the record, the witness is indicating in the direction of the accused, identifies him as Zlatko Aleksovski.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Batinic, you mention that you cooperated with Mr. Batinic (sic). What kind of cooperation was that?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Well, we discussed various business things and agreement with him. I sent him an electrician who worked with him all the time, that is, he looked after electrical installations and everything else, and we also discussed the repair of water supply to ensure the supply of water to the prison and things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned electric supply and water supply. Was it all right or --

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: No, it was irregular because pipes broke down often, but they were also repaired in time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about power supply?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Difficult at first.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Batinic, on those occasions you met Mr. Aleksovski, did you ever notice, that is, can you remember today what kind of clothes he wore? Did he wear a uniform or civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: I often met with Mr. Zlatko, both in the office and outside, and at times he truly would wear the upper part of a uniform which was very old, very shabby, ragged. I had a new uniform, for instance, and he would wear civilian trousers, and also, on a number of occasions, he was in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember if the uniform he wore had some markings there of the army he belonged to or ranks?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Oh, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if Mr. Aleksovski belonged to a military unit?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please explain what is it? That you don't know or whether he wasn't?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: He was not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Batinic, did you know the guards who worked inside the prison at Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: At one point in time, there were more guards -- no, no, no, but not in the inside. I knew the guards who worked outside but not who worked inside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the basic duty of your guards, if we may call them so, people from the Domobran company who secured the facility from the outside? What was their basic duty?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: The basic duty of people who secured the gate was to prevent people from entering the prison in an unauthorised way. They were armed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of arms did they have?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: The usual arms, rifles, M-49s.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said a Tandzara rifle?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: It's the M-49 rifle. It's an old army rifle, M-49.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From World War II?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But they also had hunting rifles?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes, who already had them, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These were their private rifles?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes, legally-owned private rifles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you had two of your guards at the gate.

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes, but there were more of them because they worked in shifts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But there were two in one shift?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes, two in one shift.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Batinic, as for the guards, your guards who secured the entry to the Kaonik facility, did you hear from them that some people would like to force their entry, some soldiers, somebody else?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember, Mr. Batinic, what facility was in the immediate vicinity of the gate inside the facility and who was located there to the left of the gate?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: It was a facility of the military police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Batinic, at the time of the armed conflicts, what was the supply situation as far as food, clothes, electricity, water as concerned in the Busovaca area? Was it regular? Was it interrupted? What can you say about it?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: It was a very difficult time, especially during the blockade from the 21st of March, 1993, because the food supplies were cut. We had to eat lentils, we all know what it is, and everybody had to eat that. Supplies of food and humanitarian aid were very poor. 14.000 refugees were then situated in the Busovaca area, the (inaudible) area of Busovaca, because the majority of the area was controlled by the Muslim forces, and so the 14.000 refugees were there and food supplies were scarce and we had to prepare our own food and take care of our own food.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you personally -- what did you eat personally?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: At home. Everybody ate at home. All members of my company ate at home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know when they were on duty, where did they eat?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Where they were at the time and where the food was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where members of the company, of the Domobran company, ate when they secured the Kaonik facility?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: At Kaonik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you personally have meals at Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the food like, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: It was good. There was meat too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether the food was prepared -- there was special food for prisoners and special food for guards, or did they eat the same food?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: They ate the same food.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Batinic, during your rounds at Kaonik, did you go into the prison itself?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What, in your opinion, were the conditions in those parts of the prison that you personally saw, and I imply hygiene conditions and how did the prisoners look like? Can you tell us something about that?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I, on several occasions, visited the prison, even during the night, together with Mr. Zlatko, and I visited my people even during the night to see how they were, and Zlatko was there frequently during the night, and on the first such occasion, when we visited the prison, there was no electricity supply in Busovaca, so Zlatko had his own lamp and we went to the prison. Zlatko said that we should visit the first cell that was next to us. I accepted that proposal. We opened the gate. There was no light and there was just a candle in the corridor, and in the cell number 1, the Mujahedin in civilian clothes were located, there were about seven or eight of them. When we entered the cell, we did not address each other by our personal name; it was the usual way of -- at the times of war. They addressed Zlatko by Asam Allah (phoen) and he asked them whether they felt well and they stood up out of respect. They looked fine to me. They were not exhausted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Batinic, you said that they were Mujahedins. Which ethnic background? They were Bosnians?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: No, they were foreigners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember, when was that?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: I don't remember the date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But it was in the prison?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Batinic, did you have the opportunity to see people, civilians, who were brought from Busovaca to Kaonik? Did you meet them?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes, because during the same night, we visited a cell where the Muslims, all the young people were located.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Batinic, did you have the opportunity to see the hangar which was situated above the prison?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Batinic, did you, by any chance, see the hygiene conditions in the prison? Was it dirty there?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: No, no, it wasn't. Because the lamp was very powerful and I could see well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see whether they had toilets there, WCs?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Not in the cell but outside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember, Mr. Batinic, whether there was heating in that building?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: There was a huge furnace in the corner that heated the entire area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of a furnace?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: The big kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was it fed on?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Timber, wood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were doing the rounds and when you visited the prison, did you see or hear that some of the prisoners were beaten, maltreated, or something of the sort?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Judging by the information from my people who secured the prison, they praised the situation, they reported to me as their commander, because they had to report to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Batinic, you said that Busovaca was surrounded by Muslim forces and that the supply situation was difficult as far as food and clothing were concerned. Tell us about the security situation in the area of Busovaca at the time. Was there any shelling, shooting?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: The situation was very difficult. There was much shelling, and the shells hit the prison too. One shell hit near or in the prison and wounded two of my members, and the second hit the very entrance of the prison, and two were wounded seriously.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean four of them?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes, four. So they were shelling, shelling the prison, and the Muslims were inside, and they knew that -- the Muslims who were shelling -- knew that their people were in the prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Batinic, do you remember whether some of the prisoners were hurt during the shelling?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does it mean actually that the prisoners were in a better position than the guards?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes. It is always secure for the people -- more secure for the people who are inside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of wounds did they sustain? Serious or slight?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: The two of them who were up there in the prison sustained lighter injuries and the people who were down there had been seriously wounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But they survived?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your people tell you, Mr. Batinic, how the guards from your company, how did they treat Muslims who were detained at Kaonik? How did they treat them?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: According to what they told me, they treated them quite well. They even gave them cigarettes. They brought them water, they gave them cigarettes, they brought them timber and wood because there was another furnace later, in a cell, so they brought them wood there. There were examples that some of them played cards because they used to be neighbours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said cigarettes first. Was it accidentally?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: No, because they were neighbours, they knew each other, and it was a custom then to offer cigarettes to your neighbours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time were cigarettes in short supply?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: At that time, you paid cigarettes in gold. A box of cigarettes was 90 Deutschemarks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the blockade?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They nevertheless shared cigarettes with them?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether they also brought food from their homes?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes, I knew about that because some of them took their neighbours home to dinner, the guards who lived near the prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did somebody complain about maltreatment, about being beaten, somebody of the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Batinic, until when were you deputy commander of the Domobran company?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Until June 1994.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you are now retired?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm retired, but I have a job in the educational sector.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you had (sic) no connection with the Domobran company?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: No, I am demobilised.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Batinic. No further questions for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mikulicic. We shall now have a 20-minute break and resume afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, Mr. Meddegoda.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, excuse me. We have to wait a moment because Mr. Aleksovski has not arrived yet. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Niemann. Now you can begin. Cross-examined by Mr. Niemann

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Batinic.

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you were in charge of the guards, the home guards at Kaonik, between February and April. What time in February did you first take up that post; can you remember the date?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: On the 28th of February, '93.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And through to what date in April? Are you able to help us with that?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: I was the deputy commander until the end of April '94.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, as deputy commander, I take it it was your duty to travel around the municipality of Busovaca to the various locations where your soldiers were guarding, doing their guard duty; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I take it that you would spend a little while at each of one of these places during the course of a day; is that how you functioned?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have a sort of central headquarters location where you would start off from, like an office or a barracks somewhere?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: An office. Yes, I did have an office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where was that located?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: In the building of forest management in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I take it that if you would think back now, I know it's very difficult because it's some time ago, but if you were to think back now and divide up your day, would you spend most of the time in the office and then the balance of the time visiting your various locations? Can you help me with that, the sort of time that you allocate in a day --

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: In the field.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you spent most of the time in the field.

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: At times my working hours took 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you spend about equal time at each place, did you?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Well, at some places more, at some places less.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, how was it that you came to find yourself drafted into the reservists? Is that something which you're given an official notification of, is it?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: I did not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry. As I understood your evidence, I think you said that in 1992, you were drafted into the reservists. I think that's what you said. If that was so, how did that come about? Did you receive a notice from somebody?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: I said that I was a volunteer in the Croatian Defence Council before I was appointed the deputy commander of a company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh. So you didn't start off as a reservist of the TO in 1992, you went straight into the HVO, is that right, as a volunteer?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is it right for me to say that at no stage with you a reservist during 1992-93, at no stage were you a reservist with the TO?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: '94, there was no Territorial Defence, there was the Croat Defence Council and the Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's right. And I think I'm right in saying, aren't I, that the remnants of the TO basically went over to the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now the rank of Major that you had, was that a rank that you carried on into the HVO, the Domobrans? I might have that wrong, the pronunciation wrong.

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I carried out the duties of a lieutenant, the company lieutenant. That was my formation duty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. Did you wear any insignia to indicate your rank?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: There were no insignia at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us about how it was the decision was made to establish the Domobran company. Was that something that was participated in by a number of the leaders in the district?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: The decision was taken on the basis of the order of the Ministry of Defence of Herceg-Bosna and then the next decision was made by the mayor of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is the mayor of the Municipality of Busovaca, is it?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was that at the time?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't know who it was in the Department of Defence that decided that this would be established, this Domobran company?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any idea who equipped it? Where did the equipment come from, what little equipment that you had in terms of military and --

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: It was personal equipment and some of it came from the regiment, from the HVO regiment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. But what HVO regiment would that be?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: I don't remember which one. I don't know the number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You, as you said, were a lieutenant, you were a deputy commander. What was the name of your commander? What was his name?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: The commander was Florijan Glavocevic, but he was more of a political leader, political function, and I was the operative man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the sort of chain of command of the Domobran after the commander and yourself? Who did they then report to? Was it directly to someone in the Department of Defence, or can you assist us by telling us a little bit about the structure of it?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: We were autonomous and subordinated to the municipal mayor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. So if you look to the ultimate leader, it would be the local mayor of Busovaca who would be your ultimate commander in chief; is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you've mentioned this question, but I just want to make sure that I do have it right. So are you saying that during 1992 at least, at no stage did you sort of take up duties as part of the TO, either in a reserve capacity or otherwise?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, did the Domobrans have any form of barracks anywhere, or was it just work on the basis that they would come from home and go back home each day?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: They came from their homes and went back home every day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
