utterances.text: Can you give us what recollections you have of your first contacts with Mr. Aleksovski when it was that the Domobrans took up the responsibility of guarding the Kaonik facility? First of all, how did the decision come about that you would assume this responsibility? Can you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember it. As the defence lines were a very dangerous area, we were afraid that they would be broken through by Muslim forces, all people of a younger age went to the defence line, and we agreed to help in that sense to prevent, that is, to prevent the entrance -- to prevent any subversive activities or anyone entering the prison and harassing prisoners and that was why we decided to set up guards at the entrance so that is when I met Zlatko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was it that decided this? Was this something decided in conjunction with Mr. Aleksovski? Is that something that you and he discussed and is that why it came about?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you first met him, did he say that he was concerned about the proximity of the prison to the frontline and the prospect of it possibly being broken into by the enemy forces?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when presented with this issue by Mr. Aleksovski, did you feel, obviously you must have done, that you had the capability of providing protection for the facility?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes. We called a meeting of the company command and took that decision.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Aleksovski attend this meeting at all?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Aleksovski explain to you precisely what it is that he wanted achieved by utilising the Domobran?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this before the decision was taken, or after?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Obviously, once he had explained what it is that he wanted, that's when you came to assess it to see whether you had the capability, no doubt?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: No, no. One explained to us what the task would be, the command then met and decided to do it this way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you then have any further discussions with Mr. Aleksovski when you actually took up your post at the camp?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the nature of the discussions? Can you help us with that? I know it's a long time ago, but if you could just sort of give us the general background of the discussion that you had with him, I would be grateful.

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: I don't remember the details.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he, for example, say to you where it is he would like the protection provided; location and things of that nature?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he discuss with you any question of limitations in terms of your soldiers coming inside the facility or anything of that nature? Did he specify anything in relation to those sorts of things?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he also talk to you about what sort of procedures would be put in place in relation to who would be permitted to enter Kaonik and who would be forbidden entry?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these are all matters that you settled with him and immediately implemented, I take it, after your men took up their position?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You spoke in your evidence about people being utilised for the purposes of labour obligations. Are you talking about --

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you talking about citizens who were still in their houses as such, if I can put it that way, during 1993, or are you talking about citizens who were being detained in the Kaonik facility?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: I referred to citizens who were not deployed as members of the Croat Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. So these were people who were still at home, I take it. They weren't in the prison.

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You may not know this, but if you do, you might help me. When it came to these people being gathered up and taken for labour duties, how was that achieved? Were they sent a written notice or did somebody go out and see them or were they told to report to the centre of the town? Do you remember how that happened?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: The Defence office of the municipality kept the records and they mobilised those people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I imagine that's how it happened. But what I'm really looking for is the process that was involved more than the official position. So how were the people notified that they would be required to assist with labour obligations? How would someone find out about that during that period, 1993, in the early part?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: By summons, or by courier and the person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. So someone would actually receive a written document and then that would direct them to go to a certain place at a certain time and then they would follow that?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And I take it that if someone was too ill or there was some other disability which affected their ability to do that, then they would have -- the obligation would be on them to provide notice to the Department of Defence that they couldn't attend?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Or to go to see a doctor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And I take it that you know of no instances at least where members of the community who were ill or injured or couldn't participate in these labour obligations, you know of no instances where they were forced to do that, notwithstanding their medical condition?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I may have had heard your evidence wrong, but I thought you said something to the effect that the Domobran were initially guarding inside the prison complex itself, not inside the cells but inside the complex of Kaonik for a while, and then that stopped. Was that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you stop? What reason did the Domobran stop guarding inside the complex itself; do you know?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: A shell fell and wounded two of my members, and ever since, we did not guard up there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when they were injured, the decision was then taken that it was too dangerous for them?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Quite.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that mean that the Domobran stopped guarding the facility altogether at that stage or just inside the complex?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: They stopped guarding around the facility and they were not inside, but after that, they guarded only the entrance to the complex which included the prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. So they continued -- after your men were injured, they continued guarding the entrance to the facility but they stopped guarding inside?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Not entrance into the facilities but the entrance to the whole complex which included the prison, that is, the entrance gate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was considered safe enough for them to stay there at the entrance gate but not safe enough for them to continue their duties guarding inside the complex itself, inside the entrance gate?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: But again a shell hit that gate too and wounded two men there also, so it was dangerous there, and yet we continued.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But notwithstanding that, the men continued their duty there. The prison complex at Kaonik was very close to the frontline, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I take it that there were other places in Busovaca, at least, municipality, which were much safer and much more distant from the frontline than the Kaonik facility?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Yes. My question was that you agreed with me that the Kaonik facility was very close in proximity to the frontline, and my next question was --

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- I take it that there were other places, locations inside the whole of the Municipality of Busovaca which were further distant from the frontline and therefore much safer; am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: That was not within my jurisdiction at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, it was not a question of jurisdiction, it was just a matter of your general knowledge. I think you would agree with me, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of that. I have no knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What you're saying is other than at Kaonik, you don't really know where the frontline was; is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: The frontline was close to Busovaca as a whole.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Do you know why the Muslim civilians were imprisoned in Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of that, but I assume it was for reasons of investigation or for security, I think, but largely because of security.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you've already told us that Kaonik wasn't exactly a very secure place. Even your own men suffered as a result of a shelling?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: But by the Muslim forces themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Tell me, we discussed a moment ago conditions regarding authorisation into the Kaonik facility. Do you remember what were the criteria, the conditions, how could somebody be permitted to enter? Can you remember what sort of conditions were imposed if somebody fronted at the gate of Kaonik and wanted to get in and met your men in the Domobran, what did they need to do to convince them that they should be given entry into the Kaonik prison?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Call the men on duty and then verify.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. So they would ring Mr. Aleksovski, would they, and say we have a gentleman here who has turned up and --

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. No. While on duty, I mean, the one that was on the duty of the facility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. So whoever that was, they would ring that person and say, "Someone's arrived here," would they?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the system work fairly successfully from your memory in terms of whether they were successful --

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: I don't remember it, really.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you did say, though, that they were successful in guarding the facility. It wasn't a failure or anything of that nature?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I take it that if they were able to keep out or had the capacity to keep out members of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, they would likewise be able to keep out HVO soldiers or other unwanted people, if necessary?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, all I'm saying is that if you had the capacity to keep out members of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina from entering the Kaonik facility, then I take it that it would be an easier task to keep out your own soldiers or soldiers of the HVO, should it be necessary to do that?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Presumably.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Aleksovski ever say to you anything about wanting to keep out members of the HVO? Did he ever say to you, "I don't want these people to enter and would you please take steps to prevent it?" Did he ever have a discussion with you like that?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the guards that worked inside the prison itself, and I'm not talking about your Domobran that worked inside the overall facility, but those prisoners who worked right inside the prison itself and the cells, do you know where they came from?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't know what organisation they belonged to, organisationally, you don't know that?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: They weren't part of my unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, no, no. Tell me: When you went and had an inspection of the gaol or you went over the gaol or prison with Mr. Aleksovski and you saw the people who you described as Mujahedins there, why did you do that? What was the purpose? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Well, we cooperated, we worked together, and it was natural to make a visit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you look at Exhibit 67 for me, please, and tell me whether or not you recognise any of these people? And it may be difficult for you to do that, so please don't be embarrassed because it's been a long time. Just looking at that for me for a moment, do you recognise any of those? You can pick it up and have a look at it if it's easier for you?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: It's very dark and it was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's fine. On this visit when you saw the Mujahedin, you said that you also had an opportunity to inspect the hygiene facilities, and I speak specifically of the toilet facilities. How did you differentiate the toilets that we use for the prisoners as oppose to the guards' toilets?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: I said that we did a round of cells and the toilets were not inside the cells but outside, and I did not go to the toilets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you didn't have the opportunity to actually inspect them for hygiene to see what their hygiene was like?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: No. I was not inspecting anything, I was simply paying a visit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You spoke in your evidence about your guards, that's guards of the Domobran, helping the prisoners, and I take it you're specifically referring to the Muslim civilian prisoners at the camp. Where did they get this --

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did they get their supply of cigarettes from, do you know, that they gave to the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Who?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your guards, the Domobran guards, that gave them to the Muslims, do you know where they got them from?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: From our unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But they didn't come in as part of humanitarian aid convoys that you know of, I take it?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also mentioned the fact that sometimes your guards even extended such hospitality to the Muslim prisoners as to take them home; do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I take it that if a guard, if one of your Domobran -- one of your guards wanted to take a prisoner home, they'd have to ask Mr. Aleksovski for permission to do that, wouldn't they? They wouldn't just take them out of the prison and walk away with the prisoner, they'd see Mr. Aleksovski first?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I might ask the question another way: You don't know of any instances where your guards were just permitted to walk in there, take a prisoner, and walk off with them, I take it, they had to get permission to do something like that, wouldn't they?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: I know they took them, but when, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Likewise, if it came to sort of meeting with the Muslim civilian prisoners that were kept inside the cells, your guards would have to get permission to go into the cells to see them, wouldn't they? They couldn't sort of walk in there; it wasn't part of their territory or jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: I do not know in what way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you saw Mr. Aleksovski at the Kaonik facility, tell me, where was his office located, offices located -- it may be more than one?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: At the entrance to the left, the first building to the left. Subsequently it was transferred to the upper part, but it was only temporarily downstairs or down there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So was this the entrance to the whole Kaonik facility, was it, that you understood his office to be?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes, the whole Kaonik complex.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you look for me, please, at Exhibit P46, and tell me whether this is the building you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm wondering if you could help me for a moment. Could you put that on the overhead projector so their Honours can see it more easily, if you move it, their Honours can't see. As best you can recall -- I know it's been a while -- but as best you're able, are you able to point with your finger at the location of the office that Mr. Aleksovski had and then the location of the office upstairs that he had by reference to the windows there? Can you do that, as best you can?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: No, I couldn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You couldn't?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: It was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So as best you can remember, he had an office downstairs at one stage and then, at a later stage, he had an office upstairs? That's the best --

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Downstairs for a very short while and very quickly he moved upstairs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for that. You mentioned the fact that you assisted Mr. Aleksovski by supplying him with an electrician at one stage. What was his name; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us what the electrician's name was?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Franjo Bagaric.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you saw the prisoners in the cell, it's your evidence, isn't it, that you actually only visited the one cell, that's the one occupied by the Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know anyone who was working at the camp by the name of Zarko Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A person by the name of Miro Maric?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, there was a Miro Maric, but the man died.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what his position was in the camp, what he did in the camp at Kaonik or --

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: No, I don't. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about a person by the name of Marko Krilic? Did you ever hear of anyone by the name of Marko Krilic?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, have you additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Maybe a couple of questions to clarify one part of the evidence during the cross-examination of my learned friend, if I may? Re-examined by Mr. Mikulicic

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Batinic, when you spoke about where Mr. Aleksovski's office was, you used the terms "up" and "down." And in the record, we have here "upstairs" and "downstairs," that is a ground floor and an upper floor. Shall we try to clarify those. Could you tell us if it is true that behind the entrance, behind the iron gate, was the building, the photograph of which you recognise here on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that you said that in that building Mr. Aleksovski's office was for a very short while?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes, for a very short while, on the ground floor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the ground floor or on the first floor?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: On the ground floor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know after Mr. Aleksovski's office was on the ground floor, where did it move after that?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: To the prison facility -- next to the prison facility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that you identified that facility by saying "up?"

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why do you say "up?"

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Because it's up the hill.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that a building which housed a prison and where there were cells, was at a higher elevation, at a higher altitude than the first building you've been referring to?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does it mean, when you said up and down, did you mean the position of the building in the area rather than parts of the building?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: The former.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Batinic, how long was Mr. Aleksovski's office in that building below?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: For a very, very short while, but I did not really -- I know that I went to see him in this building which was uphill a very short while afterwards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Batinic, do you know perhaps why did Mr. Aleksovski have the office in the first one?

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Because there were no conditions for that office in that building so it was agreed that it would be there only temporarily. That is as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VOHRAH
utterances.text: Witness, I have a question. It doesn't relate to the substance of the evidence. You mentioned that you are a member of the Domobran company. Is there a special meaning attached to the word "Domobran?"

utterances.speaker: JANKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Domobran, in World War II, were regular troops, like today -- because in the meantime, the Croatian army was formed by the Croatian Defence Council, the name we used was the Croatian Defence Council, then the people who were older took up the position in Domobran as remembering still that these were regular troops in World War II, and you know that the regiment later on became the Domobran regiment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VOHRAH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Batinic, the Chamber has no other questions for you, so it means that you have finished your testimony, giving your evidence before the Tribunal. Thank you very much, and we wish you a pleasant journey home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. We now call Stipo Juric as the witness for the Defence. (The witness entered)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: You will now read the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: You will now answer the questions which Mr. Mikulicic will put to you. Mr. Mikulicic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Mikulicic

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Juric.

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you comfortable?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My name is Mikulicic and I am counsel for the Defence of Mr. Aleksovski, and I will now pose you some questions related to the events of 1993, so I kindly ask you to answer to the best of your memory. Mr. Juric, tell us, when were you born?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: I was born on 7th of May, 1932.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: In Arias Krasno (phoen) near Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it part of the municipality of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Batinic (sic), tell us how far is the village of Krasno from Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: About seven kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your ethnic origin, Mr. Juric?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: I'm a Croat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you a believer? Are you religious?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What religion?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Roman Catholic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Juric, have you lived for your whole life in the Busovaca area?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you lived always at the same village or did you go somewhere else after you were born?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: I went to Zenica and then I returned to Kaonik where I live at present.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you live at present in Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Juric, did you go to school?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which school?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Elementary and secondary school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you go to elementary school?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: In Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that, you attended secondary school where?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: In Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of school was that?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: That was a mining industrial school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After completing the secondary school, did you find a job?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: I first went to the army to do my service at the Yugoslav People's Army. After that, I found a job in Zenica where I worked until I was retired.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you served, you were recruited to the former Yugoslav People's Army as a conscript?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any rank there?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Yes, private first class.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After doing your military service, you found the job in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of a job?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: I was a locksmith.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you worked there until you were retired?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: I was promoted. I was a foreman for diesel locomotives and I was retired in such capacity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember when did you -- when you retired?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: On 25th December, 1990.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After retirement, you went to Kaonik, you lived in Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since you lived in Kaonik, Mr. Juric, do you know of the facility that was situated there, the facility that housed -- that was used formerly by the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of a facility was that?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: It was a military facility used in the former Yugoslavia where army troops were located to have their -- I don't know what was housed in this facility besides the troops.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any opportunity of entering that facility at that time?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Batinic -- correction, Juric, I apologise, Mr. Juric, do you remember what happened at the start of 1993 when armed conflicts broke out in the Busovaca area between Croats and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: I do remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you at the time?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: At home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: In Kaonik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know, when was that exactly and what do you remember about this event?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date, but I remember that up there in Kacuni a man was killed, and the conflicts intensified since that time onwards and became full-scale conflicts between Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned the village of Kacuni where a man was killed. What was the population of Kacuni?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Predominantly Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember who was the man that was killed?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: A person by the name of Ivica Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he a Muslim or a Croat?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: A Croat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened after that?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: After that, in Busovaca itself, we saw the separation and preparation of, I don't know, the digging of trenches, and the Muslims separated themselves in the surroundings and there was an attempt at conquering Busovaca and expelling Croats, and that's how the conflict began, and this is how it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Juric, did you participate in these events? Did you take part in the defence?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: No, no, I was not involved in anything at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you later involved in any way?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Later, the Defence Council in Busovaca formed a Domobran unit that secured some facilities, and that is how I was involved and engaged too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Juric, who were members of that Domobran unit?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: For the most part, these were elderly people who were not able to go to the frontlines, and most of them were civilians and some of them had their uniforms but most of them had not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is how you got involved too?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember when it was?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: On the 1st of March in 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have some orders, some position?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Well, I was ordered to secure some facilities. That was my duty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Juric, did you have a uniform?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did other members of the Domobran units have uniforms?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Most of them wore civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any arms?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: I had an old Russian automatic weapon without any bullets, just, you know, to brandish arms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who gave it to you?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: The commander. We had no ammunition for that type of weapon. Later I received a few bullets just to have them in case I need them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said it was an old Russian automatic weapon. Where did it come from?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: I don't know. It might have come even from World War I.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this automatic weapon from World War I was the arm that you carried with no ammunition; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Juric, you said that it was your duty to secure some facilities in Busovaca; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember which facilities they were -- in which you personally were involved?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: I personally was in charge of securing the bridges, then the post building, and then I was transferred up there to secure the facility in which the people from the surrounding villages were detained. So it was my duty then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you refer to the Kaonik facility?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far is it from your home?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: About 1.000 metres, roughly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Juric, you also said that people from the surrounding villages were interned there. What villages?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Skradno, Loncari, Strane, Jelinac, these were the villages from which people were brought from and most were known to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know any of those people?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: I knew many of them because we worked together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since you knew the situation at the time of armed conflict, do you know whether, in the vicinity of these villages, there was any fighting? Was it near the frontline?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: It was precisely because of the struggles and the vicinity of the frontline that the people were brought there for their own security, and that's how they were accommodated there, because they had no where else to go on the other side, and because the fighting took place in the vicinity and that's how they were accommodated, for their own security.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. Do you know who brought them there, to Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Well, I guess the army. Who else?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember that people would come there of their own volition?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Yes, some people came there of their own free will to seek protection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From the village of Skradno?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they stay for a long time at Kaonik or was it temporarily?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: It was a temporary solution, not for a long time, because people were leaving whenever they wanted and wherever they could.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when they came to Kaonik, whether they were brought there or whether they came there of their own free will, where were they accommodated?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: In one of the buildings up there, they had a furnace there, they had food there, they were accommodated there, and this is how it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that, Mr. Juric, because you secured the facility?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was securing the facility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your duty to secure the facility from the outside or were you doing that on the inside?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: No, just from the outside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many people worked in one shift from your unit, from your Domobran company?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Two per shift.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how were you deployed?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: We worked two hour shifts and then the other two people came and we were deployed at one part of the building and the other person was on the other side, and we would allow people to go out for toilet reasons, to bring out wood, water, especially overnight to put the heat on when it was colder, we would allow them to bring the wood, we talked to them. We even gave them cigarettes, if we had to, we gave them some food, because most of the people were known to us and at least, speaking for myself, I had the same attitude towards them as towards my neighbours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they were actually your neighbours; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Juric, when you worked shifts and they lasted for two hours, what would you do after your turn? Where did you rest? Did you go home or did you stay in Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Some people who lived nearby went home because after a four-hour rest, they took up their duties again, and those who lived further away, they would stay and sleep in Kaonik or take some rest in Kaonik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Juric, you also said that people who were accommodated in the hangar which you secured, that you took them out for toilet reasons, to pick up wood, et cetera. Where was this WC situated?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Just across the building, opposite the building, nearby.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us whether, inside the building, there was electricity and whether water supply existed in the building; do you know anything about it?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't know exactly whether this existed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know anything about how these people ate, what kind of food they had?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Just like anybody else. What we ate, they ate too, depending how the situation was because nobody had enough or sufficient food.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why do you say that nobody had sufficient food?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Because we didn't have enough food because we were surrounded for months and supplies were irregular and what we had we ate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you personally eat in Kaonik or did you go home for your meals and rest?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: I ate there, down there, when I was on duty, because the situation at home was no better.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Juric, the people who were accommodated there from the surrounding villages, what was the treatment of the guards towards them? Did you see anybody maltreat them, beat them, or in any other way harass them?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: No, I have never seen that and I personally didn't do that and I never saw anyone doing it because any of the guards who could help those people in any way, they did so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you help them in any way?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, and I can even give you the exact names of the people and how I helped them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, give us the names. Please.

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: I helped Ismet Mekic from Skradno to take his things to the houses when he wanted to move to Zenica. He offered me a cow in return. I took it but then I returned it to him when -- after the liberation, and the same applied to another of my neighbours and he called me by telephone, he said he had nothing to eat because we could not sow because of the war conditions and his name was Safet (phoen), and we had some potato and we shared potatoes, he asked us whether we had some food, and this also applied to cigarettes and some food that I had in my pocket and I would give them when I was on duty, especially to the people that I knew because they would approach me and ask me if I had something to give to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Juric, whether these people had some health problems.

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, no, and those who had problems had the right to medical assistance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you personally know or do you remember whether some of those people who were up there temporarily, whether they had been seriously ill?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: I can't remember anything of the sort because I was there until 25th of April, 1993, when I was wounded, and I took a sick leave because I was wounded while on duty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know perhaps something, whether these people who were accommodated in this building, that the army would come and take them out for labour duty; do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know. When it was necessary, the army would come and take them, they would take a certain number of people according to a list, and when they completed their labour obligation, they would return them to the same building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know, since you lived in the area, whether other people from the Busovaca area had labour duties?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Yes. All the people, including Croats who could not fight, had to go trench-digging on the frontline as part of the civilian defence. It was their labour duty, and they had to go. There was no way out of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Juric, why was it necessary at the time?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: It was necessary to defend the area. It was necessary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To consolidate the frontline?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember whether, when they were returned, the people, when they were returned from labour duty, whether some of them would be injured or that some of them would be missing?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't -- I did not see anything of the sort, that somebody would be injured, and I don't know whether somebody was missing because I had no records.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand that you were not connected with that, but did you hear something of the sort?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Juric, did you hear that somebody would escape from labour duty or that somebody escaped from the Kaonik facility?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: They were instances, I heard, that some people fled, but as for the facility that we secured, nobody had escaped.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also mentioned that the civilians from the surrounding villages who were brought to Kaonik or who arrived there themselves sometimes sought medical help; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Most probably, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you personally take them for such purposes?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see that somebody from the medical centre would arrive at Kaonik; do you know what it is?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: No, I can't tell you precisely because I was on duty mostly during the night, so I had no contacts with such people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also said, Mr. Juric, that in Kaonik, that you stayed there until the 25th of April, 1993. Did I remember correctly?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why do you remember that date?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Because I was wounded on that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did it happen?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: I was on duty, fighting was in progress, and a shell hit the area outside the building, and I was hit by a piece of a shell and another person who was with me was also hit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened after that?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: After that, Mr. Zlatko came up there, he saw us, he took us in his car to Busovaca, to the ambulance, I was taken to Bila, and the other person, after seeking medical attention, went home, and I stayed at Bila after which point I went home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you referring to the Nova Bila hospital, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You then did not return to Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did, on that occasion, some of the Muslim civilians, were they injured?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that any one of them was injured during the first half of 1993 in Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: No, not that I know of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Juric, you mentioned Zlatko Aleksovski. When did you meet him first?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: I met him when I arrived there on 1st of March, and I knew that he arrived there at the end of January or beginning of February.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you recognise Mr. Aleksovski if you saw him again?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Certainly. He is sitting -- the gentleman down there, Mr. Zlatko.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: For the record, the witness was pointing to the Defendant as the person he knew by the name of Zlatko Aleksovski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, I'm interrupting you, and I'm sorry for that, but I think it is important that we now take a recess. Twenty-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, you may resume.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Lordships.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Juric, let us continue our conversation. I asked you, let me just remind you, that you met Mr. Aleksovski the first time and you said it was roughly about the time that you came to Kaonik sometime in March 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter remarks that the witness said nothing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Juric, could you tell us, how did this meeting with Mr. Aleksovski come about?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Well, it came about because I was posted there, as I was on duty, and he was also there as the prison warden, and we were down there, we were on duty, so there was contact between us, and that is how we met.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you met him, I mean Mr. Aleksovski, and later, do you remember how he was dressed?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Well, sometimes he wore a uniform, sometimes civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He had no insignia of any kind, no ranks of any kind. What uniform was that? Was it camouflage or some other uniform?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Well, no, that ordinary, the plain army uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember if, at that time, some other inhabitants in the municipality of Busovaca wore at times parts of the military uniform?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Yes. Those who were committed, those -- they'd wear uniforms. The majority of them did not have uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if Mr. Aleksovski was a member of your military unit?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if he was a member of any military unit at all?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was Mr. Aleksovski's attitude to you? I mean, how did he treat you, the guards?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: He treated us in a very correct manner, very correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you notice how he treated prisoners, the interned Muslims there?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Correctly, likewise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please clarify, what do you mean when you say "Correctly?"

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Well, I can clarify it and I would even recommend it to -- if they asked for anything to be of help, if we had a cigarette or something to offer to them, if they asked for some firewood, to allow them to bring it in; if, after a while, they would ask to go to the toilet, to let them do it, in that sense, and that is what I consider correct attitude.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Juric, if Mr. Aleksovski forbade those persons who were accommodated there be extended whatever kind of services, of course, within the framework of possibilities?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: No, he never prohibited anything, at least as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But did it seem to you -- what was the impression you had? Did Mr. Aleksovski want to help those people and make it easier for them insofar as it was possible for him?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did, within, of course, his powers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that you had been wounded because within that facility that you guarded, not far from you, a shell fell?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where this shell was fired from?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Well, from the positions of the B and H army, Miladini, Jelinak, somewhere from those sides.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did it happen only once or several times?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Several times, many times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was anyone else wounded apart from you?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Three, three more were wounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were they? Were they prisoners or ...

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Those were the guards, those who were guarding the prison, and I know the names of all of them. There were Lukin Niko, Ivo Begovic, a certain Ivica Skaro, and all three of them were wounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if any one of them, of the prisoners, of those interned civilians, were any wounded?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Not that I know of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far from Kaonik was that position that you assumed that the shell came from, the Muslim side, how far would it be?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Well, as the crow flies, perhaps 1.000, 1.500 metres, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So would it be correct to say that the position of the Kaonik facility at different intervals of time could be hit, that is, it was within the range of the Muslim fire?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Juric, you grew up in that area and lived in the area. Was there a part of Busovaca, was there a locality in the municipality of Busovaca, which at that time was not within the range of the Muslim fire?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: No, there was not a single locality, a single place, which was outside the range. They were all within the range and they were all shelled.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you also mean the town of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: The town itself, yes, shells hit the town itself and there were people killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does it also mean villages around the town of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: The villages around it, yes, the adjoining villages, certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Juric, you said that the Kaonik facility was formerly a JNA barracks. In the territory of the municipality of Busovaca, was there some other facility where a district military prison could be organised or where a large number of people could be accommodated? Was there any facility of sufficiently large size?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: No, no. There wasn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that the Kaonik facility was the only such facility in the municipality of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: The only one where those people could be accommodated. There was another army facility in a place called Draga, but only the army, the army of the former Yugoslavia, was -- and they were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the army of the former Yugoslavia left, who was in the Draga barracks?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: The HVO army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Draga facility was the barracks of the HVO army?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Juric, you have lived a long time in the area and you were also there throughout the armed conflict; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever meet a soldier with HV insignia?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see a soldier with some other insignia apart from HVO insignia?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: I only saw the military police and soldiers in the army with the HVO insignia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that your house was in the village of Kaonik, about a thousand metres away from the Kaonik facility. Did a shell hit the front of your house?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Yes, among the houses there, there was a shell which hit the ground there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was anyone wounded on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: No. No, because we were all in shelters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Juric, you said that you were a metal worker by profession, but you also can -- you are a handyman too; you can do some small repairs.

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you use those skills in the Kaonik facility?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Well, if need arose, yes, I maintained the water supply, and there were some instances when the water supply system, that is, supplying water to the prison, to the barracks, to our village, that pipeline is quite old, so pipes would burst.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you would mend them.

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: And then I went, yes, to mend them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if I understood you well, Mr. Juric, you tried in whatever way possible to help that supplies be normalised?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Yes, in every way possible, and even during the conflict, if it was possible to mend the supply -- if it was possible in order to prevent any infections, diseases or whatever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is something that I was going to ask you.

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. Fortunately, there were none.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether supplies were sometimes difficult, that they were not normal?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: You bet. But as I've said, we always tried to do all that we could in order to mend, to repair, and to normalise the situation, let me tell you, as an inhabitant of the municipality of Busovaca, as an inhabitant of the village of Kaonik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So during the conflict in the former half of 1993, did older population in the area live in the same living conditions, same supply conditions, or were some better off and others worse off?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: By and large, they all lived under equal living conditions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that apply also to Kaonik villages?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Juric. We have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Meddegoda, it is your turn. Cross-examined by Mr. Meddegoda:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Juric. Mr. Juric, you have said to this court you are presently living in Kaonik, are you?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: I live in Kaonik now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before that, you lived in Busovaca. You were born in the village of Hrasno in Busovaca where you lived for some time, and then for a while you also went to Zenica, after which you returned to Kaonik where you presently live?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: I was born in the village of Hrasno, I live in the municipality of Busovaca, and I only worked in Zenica, I only worked there and commuted between Zenica and Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you worked in the metal industry in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Zenica Steelworks, yes, heavy industry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Having lived in Busovaca a lifetime, within the municipality of Busovaca a lifetime, you knew most of the people living in that municipality?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I meant Busovaca municipality.

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Well, you could say I did, yes. I knew most of the people of my generation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was a time you said you were posted as a guard in the Kaonik camp, in the Kaonik prison, from the 1st of March, 1993.

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Yes, true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During that time, you remember there were lots of Bosniaks who were brought to Kaonik prison from the surrounding villages from the municipality of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't tell how many people were brought to the facility exactly, they were being brought in groups, so I couldn't give you an accurate figure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many groups were brought in, as far as you remember?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: In groups, at least when I was on duty, there were big groups of ten or fifteen. Depends.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who would bring them to the camp?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Who they were brought by? The military. By the military.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By which military were they being brought to the camp?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as you were aware -- you knew some of those people that were brought by the HVO military to Kaonik camp?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did know. Yes, I did know people. Yes, I did know those people who were brought in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as you know, those people who were brought in were good citizens of the community to which you belonged? The community of Busovaca, I mean.

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Doubtlessly, doubtlessly. They were decent people. They were being brought only for their protection because fighting was going on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you were sufficiently -- you said that guards, together with you, how many other guards were on duty at the Kaonik camp?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Two per shift.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Two per shift. And you belonged to the Domobran unit?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That unit was called Domobran unit because it was an older generation of men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: ... in the Domobran unit as far as you were concerned? Who was the immediate superior to whom you would report?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Our deputy commander was my predecessor, as the witness, Bagovic (sic), he was the one who decided who would be on duty when and who posted us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean the witness who testified before you?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you're referring particularly to the witness Batinic, not Bagovic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's mistake. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long was the shift of guard duty?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Two hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where would you be normally detailed for duty?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: By the facility, by the facility next to the facility, outside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "next to the facility," what did the facility comprise of?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: The facility was made of bricks and the roof and construction materials. What else could it be?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I know that. How many buildings comprised the facility? That's my question to you.

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Only one building there where those people were, in that facility, where the Muslims were, there was only one building there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you on duty inside the building, or were you on duty outside that building?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Outside. Outside the building. Outside, not inside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there other buildings within the Kaonik prison barracks facility, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: There were other buildings, there were other buildings there. Those we found after the JNA army. There were a few warehouses, barracks where the soldiers were quartered, canteen and the like.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This building that you're talking of where you were on duty outside, how far is it from the main gate, from the main entrance to the camp premises?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Some 200 to 300 metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you come along the road, are there other buildings that you would pass before you would get to that particular building that you are talking of?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Yes, I passed by them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were on duty outside the building -- how many buildings did you have to pass before coming to that particular facility?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: I pulled by two buildings, two buildings, the barracks down there and a smaller one there which was not for that purpose. Nobody could be accommodated there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By "the barracks," you mean the building with the -- the two-storey building by the gate?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Yes, the ground floor and one floor. That is the barracks. That is where the soldiers were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said, Witness, in the course of your testimony a short while ago that there were civilians who voluntarily came and sought shelter in Kaonik.

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. They did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you be able to recall or remember any of those persons, the names of those persons who came and voluntarily sought shelter?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: There were Barucija from Skradno who came on their own to get accommodation because there was fighting going on there, so to avoid it, and they had sent their womenfolk before and they had stayed to look after their houses, but when they realised it was dangerous, then they came there to be accommodated somewhere there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he the only person who came, as far as you are aware, to take shelter, or do you know others who also sought shelter in Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: There were several persons, a number of persons, but I cannot remember their names and their family names. It was some five or six years back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the only name that you can remember is the name that you just gave?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Yes, Barucija was the surname, and it was a whole village with that surname, there was a whole village up there in Skradno, a whole village, and they were all Barucijas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you said you were on duty mostly during the night, your guard shift was in the night?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Yes, you could say so, mostly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall -- do you remember what your shift hours were?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Well, every four hours, off two hours duty and four hours on, and it just depended, you know, how it came out. Sometimes I was there at 8.00, at 10.00, at 12.00, at 2.00 a.m. and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you said that you were -- knew the accused, Mr. Aleksovski?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You met him for the first time, as you said, the 1st of March, the day you got to Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you meet him often -- did you often meet him in the camp?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: I don't think it is a camp. I don't see it as a camp. It was a facility. No, he did not go up there among men who were up there. He did not go there very often. He usually spent time at his office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know where his office --

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: He would come out and go up there to see us -- to see what we were doing, how we were behaving ourselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on those occasions you would talk to him, no doubt, when he came there?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: If he asked a question, we would tell them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where his office was?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where was that?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Down there below, below this building. That was also a small building and that is where his office was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you been to that building?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, I dropped by, but I never went into any detail nor did a round of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you drop by to speak to Mr. Aleksovski when you dropped by to that building?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Only if there was something, if there was some communication to convey or something like that, but otherwise, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you had communication to convey to him, you did convey that communication to him?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: If there was a message, then why not?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I take it that there would have been instances when he spoke to you and gave you whatever instructions, depending on communications that you gave to him?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Why, of course, if we talked, he told us to take care, that we look after these people, that nothing happens to them, that nobody comes to ill-treat them, and things like that, to look after them, in that sense, those were the messages, the communications.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you helped Mr. Izet Mekic?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the circumstances in which you helped Mr. Mekic?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: I remember that he had to go to Zenica voluntarily, I mean, on his own decided and he had to take his belongings and quite a lot of them, so I helped him, you know, in a wheelbarrow, something -- I helped him drive it to the barricade, and he had a cow and he asked me to take over that cow, not to leave it there, and I refused it, I found it embarrassing, but he took that cow and brought it to my place, and I fed this cow until I could, and I sold it and I took the money to him, that is, I sent a message to him, and he came to where one could come to Gavrine Kuce and I gave the man the money I got for his cow.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was he before Zenica?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: He was from Skradvo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He had been living in Skradvo for a long time before that?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, in the camp, do you know of a guard by the name of Zarko Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: No. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you heard the name or have you heard of a guard by the name of Marko Krilic?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: No, no, I don't really know those younger people, especially in a uniform, I don't differentiate between them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Miro Maric?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: I've heard of a Miro Maric who died. To know him really, no, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was he in the camp or in the prison facility, as you say it was?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Well, he was probably down there, a guard or military police or whatever. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you also know a person by the name of Goran Medugorac?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: No, I really don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would the name Dzemo ring a bell in your mind?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Dzemo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dzemo?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: I knew a Dzemo over there at Kaonik who was there, but he also was an HVO soldier for a while.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you know another person by the same name as you by the name of Stipo Juric who was also a guard in the camp?

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: Juric?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Juric.

utterances.speaker: STIPO JURIC
utterances.text: I know no one but myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: No further questions in cross-examination, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, do you have any additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Lordships, we have no additional questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Juric, the Chamber has no further questions for you. You are finished giving your evidence here. We should like to thank you very much and wish you a pleasant journey back to your country. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Lordships, we worked today at a very accelerated rate. We did not call any other witnesses for today, so that we have no one here for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: In other words, we have to congratulate ourselves on our good work. We shall adjourn now and resume again at 9.00 tomorrow, like today. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
